request.system:
You are an extraction engine for transcripts of the Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central launch event videos.
You read machine-generated captions that carry a timestamp (seconds) per segment and you return structured JSON.

Hard rules:
- Use only what the transcript says. Do not add product knowledge, context or guesses from outside the transcript.
- Every timestamp you return must be a segment start time "t" that exists in the input, or lie inside a segment's range. Never invent timestamps.
- Quotes must be verbatim substrings of a segment text (same words, same order; you may trim the start and end). 8 to 25 words each. No paraphrasing, no fixing grammar, no stitching segments.
- Status is only what is said or shown in this video: "preview" if they say preview, public preview, beta or similar; "ga" if they say generally available, GA, out of preview, released; "announced" if it is mentioned as coming later, not in this release, roadmap; "unclear" if nothing is said. Always give the quote that proves the status, or null.
- Names of presenters are "as heard"; mark confidence low when the captions could have mangled them.
- No em-dashes anywhere in your text. Use a plain hyphen.
- Write summaries in plain language, no hype words copied from the video (no "exciting", "powerful", "seamless").

output.summary: This session introduces AL graph, a new tool in the AL tools package that builds call graphs of AL code. You first extract a meta model of caller and callee relationships once, then run as many queries on it as you like. The demo shows two queries: all callers of the HTTP client, and the calls from non-debuggable to debuggable methods. Results export as DGML for people to read or SARIF for agents to act on. The speaker says the team uses the tool internally to strengthen security, which matters more as agents make vulnerabilities easier to find.

chapters.title: Introduction: what AL graph is and why it helps
Demo: finding callers of the HTTP client
Demo: auditing non-debuggable to debuggable calls

features.name: AL graph
features.description: A new tool in the AL tools package that constructs call graphs of your code. It answers who calls whom, where external integration points and dependencies are, and which services you expose to other apps.

features.name: Meta model extraction
features.description: You first build a meta model of the caller-callee relationships in your app with an extract subcommand. It is a one-time step stored as a JSON file, and all later queries run against it.
caveats: The internal JSON representation is not something you need to worry about
prerequisites: Build the meta model before querying

features.name: AL graph query language
features.description: A fairly rich query language lets you build complex queries, such as all callers of a given object or all methods that interact with a specific table. The operations are documented on MS Learn.

features.name: DGML and SARIF export formats
features.description: Query results can be exported as DGML, a graph representation that is easy for humans to read, or as SARIF, a flatter format that an agent can act on easily.
caveats: Only the DGML export is shown in the demo

features.name: HTTP client caller query
features.description: A query exports, as DGML and excluding test files, everything that calls the HTTP client. The resulting tree shows the call paths from callers down to each HTTP method.

features.name: Non-debuggable to debuggable boundary audit
features.description: A query finds callees of non-debuggable methods so you can spot calls into debuggable code. The demo shows a non-debuggable method calling a local debuggable procedure, where a breakpoint could leak content.
